title: WAXAL: A Large-Scale Multilingual African Language Speech Corpus
claim: The data collection uses a diverse set of everyday images as prompts, covering varied topics to elicit natural speech.
layout: 8 photos in a 2x4 grid, no arrows or text
description: A two-row, four-column mosaic of eight photographs with no text, arrows or labels. Top row: a cycling race at a finish gate, wheelchair users raising joined hands in a circle, an ancient Egyptian wall painting with hieroglyphs and processing figures, and students using microscopes in a classroom. Bottom row: a group of luxury cars and a helicopter on a lot, a volleyball team posing on an orange court, a modern luxury living room interior, and elephants beside a lake with birds. The images cover sports, people, history, science, wealth, architecture and wildlife. The eye goes first to the colorful, high-contrast photos, such as the wheelchair circle and the elephants. The figure serves as a gallery of examples of the stimuli used to prompt speakers.
caption: Examples of some of the images used as prompts to elicit natural speech for the ASR dataset.
abstract: Recent advances in speech technology predominantly favor high-resource languages, leaving speakers of Sub-Saharan African languages underserved. To bridge this divide, we introduce WAXAL, an open, large-scale speech dataset spanning 27 African languages representing over 100 million speakers. WAXAL comprises over 14,100 hours of speech collected in partnership with African academic and community organizations to build local research capacity: an Automatic Speech Recognition (ASR) corpus with 2,340 hours of transcribed, image-prompted natural speech across 19 languages (plus ~11,760 untranscribed hours) and a studio-quality Text-to-Speech (TTS) corpus of ~247 hours across 15 language configurations. We empirically benchmark three architecturally distinct ASR models -- Gemma 3n 2B, Whisper-Large-v3, and MMS-1B-all -- across the 19 ASR languages on strictly speaker-disjoint splits. Fine-tuning on WAXAL yields substantial gains, reducing macro-average WER by up to 58% for Whisper-Large-v3, 56% for Gemma 3n 2B, and 17% for MMS-1B-all (and Character Error Rate by up to 70%). WAXAL-fine-tuned models generalize zero-shot to three out-of-distribution benchmarks: FLEURS, Mozilla Common Voice, and Sunbird SALT. Finally, an LLM-as-judge semantic evaluation confirms that fine-tuning preserves speaker intent beyond surface-level transcription metrics. WAXAL is released at https://huggingface.co/datasets/google/WaxalNLP.
